[![](data:image/png;base64,)](http://crossmark.crossref.org/dialog/?doi=10.1016/j.carbpol.2025.123297&domain=pdf)Adsorption performance and mechanism of a novel composite based on β-cyclodextrin polymer and chitosan: Selective and rapid removal of acid orange 7

Jakub Lagiewka [a](#_bookmark0),[\*](#_bookmark2), Anna Pajdak [b](#_bookmark1), Iwona Zawierucha [a](#_bookmark0)

a _Institute of Chemistry, Faculty of Science and Technology, Jan Dlugosz University in Czestochowa, Czestochowa 42-200, Poland_

b _Strata Mechanics Research Institute, Polish Academy of Sciences, 30-059 Krakow, Poland_

A R T I C L E I N F O

_Keywords:_ Cyclodextrins Cyclodextrin polymers Chitosan

Organic dyes Water treatment

A B S T R A C T

Continuous production of textiles results in the emission of organic dyes into the aquatic environment. The application of cyclodextrin based adsorbent allows the efficient, rapid and selective removal of organic pollutants from aqueous solutions. The present study deals with the synthesis of adsorptive composite based on the poly (β-cyclodextrin-perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic dianhydride) network and chitosan through ionic crosslinking. The electrostatic interactions, between the carboxylate group of cyclodextrin polymer and the amino group of chitosan, allowed to form the material. The adsorption studies were carried out for acid orange 7 (AO7) removal as an example of anionic dye. The highest removal provided a mass ratio 1:4 of cyclodextrin polymer and chi-tosan, which was 5-times greater than for chitosan. The adsorption capacity was 384.61 mg/g according to the Langmuir model. The rapid adsorption after 1 min exhibited 95.6 % of removal. Comparison of dyes and metal ions showed the preference of anionic dyes over other pollutants, this selectivity was only for the composite and induced by the addition of cyclodextrin polymer. The removal mechanism was based on electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding and inclusion complexation. The presented adsorptive composite is a promising tool for treatment of (waster)water from organic dyes.

# Introduction

Wastewater production has evolved with dye and printing technol-ogy to become one of the major sources of soil and water contamination ([Cova et al., 2021](#_bookmark26)). Most of the dyes in textile industries are based on organic compounds that characterise carcinogenic and mutagenic properties. In addition, the organic dyes are dangerous for aquatic flora and fauna, because of reduced visibility and limited photosynthesis ([Berradi et al., 2019](#_bookmark25); [Ismail et al., 2019](#_bookmark43)). Thus, the proper strategies for dye removal from aqueous environments is crucial for the safety of ecosystems.

Nowadays, there are several advanced techniques for their removal: membrane separation ([Z˙ yłła et al., 2022](#_bookmark83)), biological treatment ([Alfonso-](#_bookmark19)

[Muniozguren et al., 2021](#_bookmark19)), advanced oxidation processes (AOP) ([Bermúdez et al., 2021](#_bookmark24)), photocatalysis ([Ravindra et al., 2023](#_bookmark61)) and adsorption ([Lagiewka et al., 2023](#_bookmark51)). The above mentioned techniques, except adsorption, are using expensive material, time consuming, complex in their application, need strict conditions for the biological

process. Therefore, adsorption seems to be the most promising way to remove organic pollutants due to low cost, easy operation, rapid and high efficiency.

One of the most harmful group of dyes are azo compounds (-N=N-),

which are estimated as 60–70 % of all commercial dyes. The main issues with their disposal are long-lasting or the lack of biodegradation, and stability ([Strebel et al., 2024](#_bookmark68)). Many azo dyes are known for their anionic character with sulphonate group (SO—). Most of them are applied in wool or silk dyeing for leather or paper coloration, a good example is Acid Orange 7 (AO7) ([Greluk & Hubicki, 2011](#_bookmark38)). Exposure to AO7 can induce severe headaches, dermatitis, anaemia, its metabolite can cause bladder tumours. Thus, finding a novel solution for its removal can be an important aspect of environmental engineering and public health ([Greluk & Hubicki, 2011](#_bookmark38)).

3

Synthesis of a novel adsorbent towards the efficient removal of azo dyes require the application of the proper material that could provide increased adsorption capacity, rapid removal and strong affinity to organic compounds. Such adsorbents can be obtained from

polysaccharides e.g. cyclodextrins (CDs) or chitosan, these biopolymers are a cheap, easily accessible, biodegradable resource for adsorbents.

The CDs are oligosaccharides, with a macrocyclic structure; mostly with six, seven or eight glucose e.g. α-CD, β-CD and γ-CD. These su-pramolecular rings form inclusion complexes with organic compounds, mostly in drug delivery ([Jambhekar & Breen, 2016](#_bookmark44); [Szejtli, 1998](#_bookmark69)). The presence of a CD cavity in the adsorbent provides a strong organophilic and selective character with a high removal efficiency or even rapid kinetics. These features are characteristic for multifunctional materials containing many different functional groups like the CD cavity, hydroxyl groups, ionisable group or even aromatic rings ([Alsbaiee et al., 2016](#_bookmark21); [Morin-Crini et al., 2018](#_bookmark54)). The CD in multifunctional material behaves like a receptor with a strong ability to recognise and bind sorbate mol-ecules depending on their chemical structure/character ([Lagiewka et al.,](#_bookmark51) [2023](#_bookmark51)). For instance, the polymer based on β-CD and tetra-fluoroterephthalonitrile was capable of rapidly removing organic pol-lutants (e.g. bisphenol A, propranolol hydrochloride) after 0.5 min or 1 min in the range of 65–95 % ([Alsbaiee et al., 2016](#_bookmark21)). Further, the nitrile groups were replaced with carboxyl/amine groups in order to remove methylene blue (MB) ([Jiang et al., 2019](#_bookmark45)) and perfluoroalkyl compounds ([Klemes et al., 2019](#_bookmark48)). The other type of CD adsorbent was the poly(β-CD-

3,3′,4,4′-biphenyltetracarboxylic dianhydride) network designed by

[Lagiewka et al. (2023)](#_bookmark51), containing CD cavity, biphenyl units and

carboxylate groups, which allows the rapid removal of the methylene blue at 84 % after 1 min.

Chitosan based materials are a second type of materials based on naturally derived chitosan from chitin. The chitosan material is char-acterised by strong adsorption properties towards metal ions due to nitrogen atom and hydroxyl groups through coordination bonds or hydrogen bonding towards organic dyes. Such materials do not provide rapid or selective adsorption and can be accessed through chitosan's modification. For instance, carboxymethylation and partial cross-linking of chitosan increased the adsorption capacities for the removal of organic pollutants (e.g. methylene blue) and divalent metal ions (e.g. cadmium ions) ([Doshi et al., 2018](#_bookmark30)). The other adsorbent based on chi-tosan was based on clinoptilolite and cetyltrimethylammonium bromide for the removal of methyl orange (MO). The formation of a composite provided access to NH+ group for binding the sulphonated group of MO, increased adsorption efficiency and total removal after 10 min ([Babazadeh et al., 2021](#_bookmark22)). The other composite was obtained through the addition of iron nanoparticles and microalgae biomass with increased adsorption in the range of 125.6–753.2 mg/g for antibiotics e.g. tetra-cycline ([Mirizadeh et al., 2024](#_bookmark53)).

3

Thus, the combination of CD and chitosan into one material could provide new fascinating adsorption properties that were unavailable before e.g.: cross-linked chitosan/β-Cyclodextrin composite ([Jiang et al.,](#_bookmark46) [2018](#_bookmark46)), chitosan/β-Cyclodextrin composite impregnated with lantha-nium ions (La3+) ([Preethi & Meenakshi, 2018](#_bookmark59)), chitosan and β–cyclodextrin crosslinked with glutaraldehyde ([Verma et al., 2022](#_bookmark72)), multifunctional β-cyclodextrin-EDTA-chitosan polymer ([Verma et al.,](#_bookmark73) [2023](#_bookmark73)). The presented work is expanding the library of adsorptive ma-terial based on CD or/and chitosan. The hypothesis for this research is: ionic crosslinking of carboxylated β-cyclodextrin polymer with chitosan forms a novel adsorbent with enhanced and selective adsorption of anionic dyes.

In order to prove the hypothesis, the novel adsorptive composite based on the poly(β-cyclodextrin-perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic dia-nhydride) network and chitosan was prepared with improved properties such as highly efficient, rapid and selective removal of AO7. The com-posite was synthesised by ionic crosslinking of the novel poly(β-cyclo-dextrin-perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic dianhydride) network and chitosan, where the polymeric CD network was the source of the nega-tively charged carboxylate group and chitosan was the source of the positively charged amino group. The PTCDA was applied as a cross-linker in the synthesis of the CD polymeric network. It helps to keep the process cost-effective while enhancing the molecular weight, making it easier to

integrate into the chitosan matrix. The structure of PTCDA is similar to that of nanographene particles, which are polycyclic flat aromatic com-pounds. This similarity allows PTCDA to effectively bind dye molecules through π-electron interactions. The material was characterised with spectral methods to provide information about its molecular structure and mechanism of formation. The adsorption processes were studied in the case of AO7 as an example of anionic azo dyes to determine the in-fluence of different parameters (e.g. time, pH). The molecular mechanism for AO7 binding was based on spectral methods and selectivity for the better explanation of the mechanism of action. This paper is going to design a novel type of cyclodextrin and chitosan based adsorbent.

# Materials and methods

- 1.  _Materials_

Crystalline β-Cyclodextrin, perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic dianhy-dride (PTCDA), _N_,_N_\-dimethylformamide (DMF) were provided by Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MI, USA. Chitosan (catalog number-ACRO349050500, degree of purity was 98 %, degree of deacetylation was 75 %, _Mw_ was 200 kDa) was purchased from Acros Organics, Pittsburgh, USA. NaCl, MgSO4, CaH2, 0.1 M HCl/NaOH, acetone, glacial acetic acid, Acid Orange 7 were obtained from Chempur, Krupski Mlyn, Poland. NaH (60 % sus-pension in paraffin oil) was obtained from MERCK, Darmstadt, Germany. The 1000 mg/L solutions of Zn2+, Ni2+ and Cd2+ were obtained from SPEX Certiprep, USA. The β-CD, DMF, NaH was purified prior to use according to [Lagiewka et al. (2023)](#_bookmark51).

- 1.  _Characterisation and measurement_

The NMR spectra were obtained by a Bruker Advance 3HD 400 MHz spectrometer for 1H and 13C, with D2O. The FT-IR spectra were recorded on a Nicolet-Nexus spectrometer in a range of 4000–400 cm—1 with the KBr pellet method. The molecular weight of the novel polymer was determined with gel permeation chromatography with size-exclusion chromatography (GPC/SEC) on a 1260 Infinity II GPC/SEC System supplied with refractive index (RI) detector. The GPC tests were per-formed at a flow rate of 1.0 mL/min and using 0.02 % NaN3 aqueous solution as the eluent and PLaquagel-OH Mixed-H 300 mm and 7.5 mm chromatographic column as stationary phase (Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). The chemical composition of the surface was evaluated with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) on an electron spectrometer (Specs). The microstructure analysis and elemental composition of surface was performed on a scanning electron micro-scope (VEGA3 TESCAN). The pore structure, size and specific surface area were characterised by low-temperature gas (nitrogen) adsorption on ASAP 2020 (Micromeritics). The phase composition/crystallinity was measured on an X-Ray diffractometer (Rigaku MiniFlex 600). Thermal properties (stability, phase transitions) were evaluated on a thermog-ravimeter (TGA/DSC3, Mettler Toledo) and differential scanning calo-rimeter (DSC3, Mettler Toledo). The dyes concentrations were determined on a spectrophotometer UV-VIS Shimadzu 2401. The metal ions concentrations were determined on an atomic emission spectrom-eter with microwave plasma Agilent 4210 MP-AES. The chemical sta-bility was evaluated through mixing 10 mg of composite with 10 mL of solutions with different pH in a range: 2–12; then filtered and weighted after 1, 2 and 24 h. Above mentioned characterisation methods/pro-tocols were carried out according to [Lagiewka et al. (2023)](#_bookmark51), except for NMR spectroscopy and GPC/SEC ([Girek et al., 2000](#_bookmark37); [Girek et al., 2020](#_bookmark35)).

- 1.  _Synthesis of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network_

The synthesis protocol of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network was slightly modified from methods developed by [Girek et al. (2000)](#_bookmark37) and [Lagiewka et al. (2023)](#_bookmark51).

The dry β-CD (1.135 g, 1 mmol) was placed in a round bottomed flask

and dissolved with 25 mL of freshly dried DMF. Further, the NaH (0.096 g, 4 mmol) was slowly added to the mixture and magnetically stirred for 24 h at room temperature. Then, the PTCDA (1.569 g, 4 mmol) was

- 1.  _Synthesis of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite_

The synthesis protocol of the composite was based on the method-ology developed by [Ostrowska-Czubenko and Gierszewska-Druz˙yn´ska](#_bookmark57) [(2009)](#_bookmark57). The composite was based on the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network and chitosan through ionic crosslinking/electrostatic interactions, where the chitosan was a matrix of the adsorbent.

Initially, the reusability studies were performed to determine the most desorptive mixture. Firstly, the most optimal composition was determined through application of mixture: organic solvent (methanol,

ethanol or acetone) with aqueous solution (0.01 M HCl or NaOH) in volume ratio of 3:1. The most effective desorptive mixture was meth-anol/0.01 M NaOH; the optimal volume ratio was then studied in the range of 1:1 to 4:1.

In order to determine the possible reusability of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite, the estimation of adsorption and desorption cycles was carried out. Based on the performed experiments, the most efficient regeneration solution was a mixture of methanol/0.01 M NaOH in a volume ratio 3:1.

The 0.01 g of adsorbent was mixed with 10 mL of 100 mg/L aqueous solution of AO7 for 60 min. The stock solution was filtered, then the adsorbent was left to dry overnight. Further, the 0.01 g of adsorbent was mixed with 20 mL of regeneration solution for 120 min, then filtered and left to dry overnight. These adsorption-desorption cycles were carried out five times.

# Results and discussion

- 1.  _Synthesis of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network_

The poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network was synthesised by oxyanion strat-egy ([Girek et al., 2000](#_bookmark37); [Lagiewka et al., 2023](#_bookmark51)), where β-CD was activated through the reaction with NaH and the formation of highly reactive oxyanion ([Fig. 1](#_bookmark3)). Then, CD oxyanion attacked the anhydride rings of PTCDA through nucleophilic substitution. Ring opening formed an ester bond, as a linkage between β-CD and PTCDA, and left a free carboxylate group. The synthesised polymer possessed a network structure due to the 3-dimensional geometry of CD and many reactive sites/hydroxyl groups in CD. The molar ratio for CD:NaH:PTCDA was 1:4:4 and pro-vided sufficient results, where four activated hydroxyl groups of CD reacted with PTCDA as two functional crosslinking agents. The lower molar ratio below 4 would not provide a network structure, this could result in a chain/linear like structure with less complexed binding sites and low molecular weight. The low molecular weight could not provide precipitation and a stable complex within the chitosan matrix due to its easy leaching out. The cross-linking reaction was performed with yield of 82.5 %.

The molecular structure of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network was analysed with 1H/13C NMR, FT-IR spectroscopy and GPC. The atom numbering (red colour) in [Fig. 1](#_bookmark3) is applied for NMR analysis in order to better visualise and explain the molecular structure.

1H NMR in Fig. S1 shows the β-CD structure in the range of

3.44–5.00 ppm and the perylene units in the range of 7.52–8.42 ppm. The H-6 from the primary carbon atoms and H-5 are assigned to the range of 3.72–3.80 ppm. The H-4 and H-1 from the carbon atoms next to the glycosidic linkage correspond to signals at 3.45 ppm and 4.93 ppm. The H-2 and H-3 from the secondary carbon atoms are connected to signals 3.54–3.86 ppm ([Ali et al., 2007](#_bookmark20)). The aromatic regions is divided in two parts 7.52–7.86 ppm and 8.36–8.42 ppm. The first part comes from the hydrogen atoms H closer to the inner core of the perylene unit. The second part comes from the hydrogen atoms next to the carbonyl

bond of the carboxyl group/ester bond.

13C NMR in Fig. S2 shows three parts of signals in the range of 60–102 ppm from β-CD, 120–138 ppm from the perylene units, and 171–177 ppm from the carbonyl bonds of the ester linkage/carboxyl group. Six signals corresponding to each of the carbon atoms of the glucose units are found in the range of 60–105 ppm. The first signal at 60 ppm is from the C6 primary carbon atoms from the wider rim. Next, the signals at 71–73 ppm are from C2, C3 and C5 from the secondary carbon atoms, respectively. The last signals at 81 ppm and 102 ppm refer to C4 and C1 from the glycosidic linkage, respectively. The next part from the perylene units contains 6 signals in spite of the 8 carbon atoms from the perylene, presumably due to the relaxation time and other intermolecular forces in the solutions. The peaks at 121 ppm and 128–129 ppm refers to the carbon atoms F, I, _J_ and B/G found at the

β-carbon atoms to the carbonyl group. The carbon atom D/E from the

bay region refer to 131 ppm, while the X/A from the α-carbon atoms to the carbonyl group are found at 138 ppm. The last part, from the carbonyl groups, refers to atom from the ester or carboxylate group that are at 171 ppm and 177 ppm.

FT-IR spectroscopy for β-CD, PTCDA and the polymeric network is presented in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark4)A. The presence of β-CD cavity was confirmed with a strong wide band at 3392 cm—1 referring to stretching vibrations of O–H bonds, small band at 2924 cm—1 referring to stretching vibrations of C–H, and three peaks in the range 1158–1028 cm—1 referring to stretching vibrations of β-CD's glucose unit ([Ge et al., 2011](#_bookmark34)). The aro-matic skeleton from the perylene was confirmed by small band at 1550–1450 cm—1 ([Scholz et al., 2003](#_bookmark65)). The carbonyl bond C–O is provided by the band at 1664 cm—1 and corresponds to ester bonds and anhydride rings ([Hietpas & Allara, 1998](#_bookmark39); [Scholz et al., 2003](#_bookmark65)).

The average molecular weight (_Mw_) was analysed on GPC where the eluent was 0.02 % NaN3. with a flow rate 1 mL/min. As seen in Fig. S3, the analysed compounds contained two polymeric fractions with a maximum retention time at 7.88 min and 8.87 min. The _Mw_ for the first and second elution were 929 kDa and 235 kDa, which characterise high molecular weight polymers due to the presence of CD and PTCDA units in the polymeric network structure. These high _Mw_ are characteristic to CD polymers due to the high molecular weight for one β-CD molecule of

1.13 kDa ([Girek et al., 2000](#_bookmark37); [Girek et al., 2005](#_bookmark36)). According to Fig. S3, there are only two polymeric fractions, but there is lack of fractions before 7.5 and after 9.2 min. Thus, it indicates fully reacted CD with PTCDA, especially lack of smaller fraction (around 1.1. kDa for β-CD). The polymerisation of CD molecules increases their _Mw_ after the addi-tion of only few of them. However, such solubility in this case is pro-vided by the presence of hydroxyl groups in CD units as well as the formation of the carboxylate group from anhydride rings, which favours strong hydrophilic interactions ([Girek et al., 2020](#_bookmark35)).

The studied composition of the fraction and synthesis method was assumed as the most optimal after conducted different experiments (synthesis, composite formation/stability, adsorption efficiency) and some characteristic features. Firstly, all substrates completely reacted and formed gel after 24 h, which means the highest molecular weight of

According to initial studies on composite for-mation, the ratio of CD to PTCDA should not be below 1:4; otherwise, the composite cannot form and remain stable in solutions. Higher ratios produced similar mass weights (yields below 82.5 %) or only slightly better results. However, in some cases, the composites formed later exhibited similar or weaker adsorption efficiencies. Therefore, using a higher ratio may not be economically viable for effective removal. Finally, this synthesis protocol provided the poly(β-cyclodextrin-per-ylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic dianhydride) network capable of forming the most stable adsorptive composite with chitosan.

- 1.  _Synthesis and characterisation the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/ chitosan composite_

The composite preparation was carried out via ionic crosslinking with the protocol developed by [Ostrowska-Czubenko and Gierszewska-Druz˙yn´ska (2009)](#_bookmark57). This ionic crosslinking considered the electrostatic interaction between two polymeric compounds, where the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network was negatively charged from the carboxylate groups and the dissolved chitosan positively charged from the amino groups. The preparation and possible structure of the composite is shown in

[Fig. 3](#_bookmark5), where the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network is responsible for con-necting of chitosan chains and the formation of a more complexed network. The change of colour into red after 1 h of stirring confirmed the reaction between the two polymers. After removal of solvents (water and acetic acid), a red solid was formed and washed with water to remove unreacted particles. The red solid was ground in a mortar due to very crucible properties and formed a fine powder for further studies. Cost of this composite is estimated around 1522 USD per 1 kg, which is close to price of chitosan (around 1592 USD per 1 kg) and β-CD (around 1970 USD per 1 kg). In spite of use PTCDA estimated around 2058 USD per 1 kg, which price is close to carbohydrate components, the appli-cation of NaH (278 USD per 1 kg) allowed to slightly decrease price of CD, chitosan and PTCDA to obtain adsorbent with relatively low price. The composition and formation mechanism of the adsorbent were evaluated through comparison with the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network and pristine chitosan, the composite FT-IR spectra in [Fig. 2](#_bookmark4)B is a combination of both components. The strong and wide band at 3392 cm—1 refers to stretching vibrations of O–H and N–H bonds from the β-CD, the carboxylate group of the polymer and chitosan. The band at 3392 cm—1 for the composite was observed as less intensive and narrower compared to chitosan, which indicates the participation of hydrogen bonding and presumably electrostatic interactions from OH, COO—, NH and/or NH+. The C–H bonds is present without significant changes for stretching

vibrations at 2924 cm—1 referring to the alkyl chains of all the materials. The band at 1664 cm—1 has become less intensive from chitosan and slightly redshifted to 1654 cm—1, while stronger than for the polymeric network. On the other hand, the band at 1584 cm—1 from the N–H bond has become stronger and redshifted to 1562 cm—1, linked to the for-mation of N+\-H. Observations from C–O and N–H indicates their participation in the material formation through electrostatic interaction COO— ••• NH+ ([Ostrowska-Czubenko & Gierszewska-Druz˙yn´ska, 2009](#_bookmark57)). 3

The XPS analysis determined the chemical composition of the surface. As seen in [Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)A, the survey spectra indicates the presence of C, O and N atoms on the adsorbent surface, which consists of the poly(β-cyclodex-trin-perylene-3,4,9,10-tetracarboxylic dianhydride) network and chito-san. The C1s region ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)B) consists of bands at 284.0 eV, 285.5 eV and

287.1 eV, which refers to C–C, Caryl, C–O, C–N, C–O, O-C-O ([Huang,](#_bookmark42)

[Chai, et al., 2020](#_bookmark42); [Vieira et al., 2011](#_bookmark74)). The O1s region ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)C) contains two signals at 531.7 eV and 532.7 eV; these signals correspond to O–C and O–C from anhydride rings, carboxyl groups and ester bonds ([Turco](#_bookmark71) [et al., 2018](#_bookmark71)). The last regions as N1s ([Fig. 4](#_bookmark6)D) exhibits two significant bands at 398.9 eV and 400.4 eV, both signals can refer to N–C and N+ for the range 396–403 eV ([Vieira et al., 2011](#_bookmark74)).

The chemical stability was evaluated in a pH range of 2–12 with different solutions of HCl and NaOH to understand the hydrolytic pro-cess or solubilisation of polymers in the composite, which determine material stability. The changes in mass of the composite were observed at a pH of 2, 3, 11 and 12 as seen in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)A. The pH of 3 and 11 induce degradation of the composition only after 24 h, thus the pH below 3 and above 11 cannot be applied for adsorption processes due to the lack of stability during 1 or 2 h. For acidic environments, the results are con-nected to the solubilisation of the chitosan matrix through the strong dissolving influence of H+ ions. The alkaline environment induces hy-drolysis of the ester bond from the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network and its depolymerisation, which releases CD molecules into aqueous solutions

([Rowe et al., 2016](#_bookmark63)). Therefore, the composite can be applied to the adsorption process during 1 or 2 h in a pH range of 3–11.

The evaluation of XRD patterns in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)B and Fig. S4 indicated the presence of “_halo motif”_ with three peaks at 8◦, 12◦ and 20◦ for the composite. This motif indicates domination of the amorphous structure in materials due to the addition of different polymeric material, which could form a semicrystalline phase due to the non-uniform composition of all materials and different mass fractions of the same compounds. The 8◦ and 12◦ is present in polymeric network and its components, while the 20◦ is a characteristic band for chitosan.

Thermal analysis was performed with TGA and DSC techniques to evaluate the thermal stability and the thermal properties of the com-posite, and DTG was applied to thoroughly investigate thermal degra-dation. The DTG/TGA in [Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)C showed the first weight loss of 15 % in a temperature range of 30–100 ◦C due to evaporation of solvents residues The next significant step at 250–350 ◦C was connected to chitosan degradation (Fig. S5B), which refers to the most intensive weight loss from the matrix ([Neto et al., 2005](#_bookmark55)). It is also connected to depolymer-isation process through cleavage of the ester linkage and degradation of β-CD molecules according to Fig. S5A-S5C ([Lagiewka et al., 2023](#_bookmark51); [Sabzi](#_bookmark64) [& Kiasat, 2018](#_bookmark64)). The steps in the range 450–600 ◦C are responsible for the degradation of perylene units from polymer residues as seen in Fig. S5D. DSC analysis of the composite ([Fig. 5](#_bookmark7)D), indicated dehydration as the first endothermic process around 60–100 ◦C, even in chitosan and the polymeric network (Fig. S6A-S6B). The next process is exothermic in the range of 250–325 ◦C and refers to the depolymerisation process of chitosan or CD units and the polymeric network (Fig. S6C). The DSC curve of the composite is similar to chitosan and the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network (Fig. S6A-S6B), thus the composite is still characterised simi-larly to the carbohydrate types of materials in spite of aromatic units (Fig. S6D).

Morphology analysis and surface composition was evaluated with SEM and EDX. According to Fig. S7A, the SEM image shows grouped particles with non-homogenous surfaces. The particles exhibit different

According to Fig. S7B and Table S1, the content of elements on adsorbent surfaces are connected to adsorbent composition: poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network, chitosan. - 1.  _Effect of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network on adsorption efficiency_

The influence of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network on adsorption of AO7 by the chitosan based composite was evaluated in a concentration range of 0–0.1 wt% of poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network solution. Based on results from [Table 1](#_bookmark8), the most efficient adsorption was 98.9 % and was observed for 20 % of the content of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network. This value was 5-times greater than for pure chitosan, which only succeeded in 19.4 % removal. Thus, the addition of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network to chitosan allowed the formation of a more effective adsorbent than native chitosan.

The higher and lower contents of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network in the chitosan matrix resulted in lowered adsorption efficiency (_A.E.)_, below 97.7 %. It indicates the most optimal composition of this ionically cross-linked composite, with 20 % of the polymeric CD network and 80

- 1.  _Dye concentration and adsorption isotherms_

Initially, the influence of AO7 concentration on adsorption efficiency was evaluated in the range 10–500 mg/L. The results in [Fig. 6](#_bookmark9)A indicate the most efficient removal for AO7 concentration of 100 mg/L is around

98.9 %. This level of AO7 will be considered further to understand other optimizing and limiting factors on adsorption processes. The concen-trations of AO7 in the ranges 10–75 and 200–300 mg/L are found as less effective, but still can be treated with the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/

The equilibrium/possible mechanism of adsorption was studied with the Langmuir and Freundlich models. Both models ([Fig. 6](#_bookmark9)B-C), are in agreement with the obtained results due to coefficient of determination _R2_ value above 0.96. However, only the Langmuir model provides an _R2_ value of 0.996 indicating a better fit than the Freundlich model with an _R2_ value of 0.961. Thus, the adsorption is based on the formation of a monolayer on the adsorbent surface, where binding sites characterise equivalent structure. Based on [Table 2](#_bookmark11), the adsorption capacity of AO7 by the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite is 384.61 mg/g; The _n_ coefficient from the Freundlich model is 3.13, which indicates the reversible character of the process. However, Freundlich model cannot be fully considered as the most adequate due to the much lower _R2_

value.

The poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite is characterised by a very high _qmax_ of 384.61 mg/g for AO7 adsorption. Based on [Table 3](#_bookmark10), the highest efficiency was 1379 mg/g and observed for Amberlite IRA-959 functionalised with the trimethylammonium. The

However, similar levels of adsorption capacity like in our case were for the Orange peel magnetic activated carbon ([Khalil et al., 2024](#_bookmark47)) and Sulphonated man-darin biochar ([Eleryan et al., 2024](#_bookmark31)) of around 312–357 mg/g, which were formed through carbonisation of natural resources like fruits. Thus, the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite seems to be a good replacement for these materials in the application of natural resources. The other (nano)composites, e.g. mesoporous TiO2 ([Xu et al., 2011](#_bookmark75)), magnetite/carbon ([Nistor et al., 2022](#_bookmark56)) and polypyrrole/nanosilica ([Sillanpa¨a¨a et al., 2023](#_bookmark66)) had weaker adsorption efficiency in spite of containing carbonaceous materials. In presented measurements, the presence of perylene units provided stronger adsorption efficiency through π-electron interaction than for carbonaceous materials like biochar, polymers or nanoparticles. One of the CD based materials for AO7 removal is hydrogel based on epichlorohydrin and β-CD, which was on a similar level of 132 mg/g similar to the previously mentioned composite ([Zhang et al., 2017](#_bookmark81)). To sum up, the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite is characterised as one of the efficient materials while these results come from a combination of perylene units, CD and chitosan.

- 1.  _Adsorbent dosage influence on removal_

The optimisation of adsorption of AO7 was studied by adding different mass dosages of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite in the range of 0.001–0.03 g, where the concentration of AO7

was 100 mg/L. The analysis was performed to determine the most effi-cient ratio of mass sorbent to volume of aqueous solution in the range of 0.1–3 g/L with 10 mL volume of solutions as a constant. Based on [Fig. 6](#_bookmark9)D, the 90 % of adsorption was exceed by 5, 7, 10 and 20 mg, where only 10 and 20 mg provided almost full removal. The adsorption effi-ciency is highest only for the lower dosages because bigger particles result in parallel adsorption-desorption. In addition, the aggregation of

dye molecules on binding sites can results in lengthening the diffusion path ([Garg et al., 2004](#_bookmark33)). The application of a smaller dosage (<10 mg) results in _A.E._ around 83 % due to the lower number of adsorbent

molecules and its catching groups of AO7 molecules. As shown in the [Fig. 6](#_bookmark9)D the optimal ratio for adsorbent mass to volume aqueous solution is 1 mg/mL.

- 1.  _Time of adsorbent contact and adsorption kinetics_

The evaluation of time on the adsorption process was analysed in the range of 0–120 min for 100 mg/L of concentration. The process was described with the following models: _A.E._ \= _f(Time)_, PSO and PFO models; all models are seen in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark12)A-C, respectively. The calculated parameters for the PSO and PFO models are found in [Table 4](#_bookmark13).

As seen in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark12)A, the _A.E._ of AO7 on the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite is remarkably rapid, observed at 95.6 % of adsorption after 1 min. The range of 2–60 min shows small removal increase from 96.3 % up to 98.9 %. The process exhibits equilibrium at 60 min and its endpoint due to a small decrease of _A.E._ after 60 min. After 60 min, complete saturation of the binding site is observed. This

composite characterises quicker adsorption of organic pollutants than chitosan-EDTA-β-cyclodextrin ([Zhao et al., 2017](#_bookmark82)) or cross-linked chito-san/β-CD with glutaralaldehyde ([Jiang et al., 2018](#_bookmark46)). Both materials reached equilibrium towards organic pollutants after 180 min, after 5 min removal is around 35–75 %. Adsorbents with one or two types of binding sites can be effective for prolonged adsorption processes. On the other hand, the material with a multifunctional character, where many different functional groups are present, rapid removal is observed ([Lagiewka et al., 2023](#_bookmark51)). Similar ultra-rapid removal after 0.5 min to-wards different organic pollutants was achieved by poly(CD-tetrafluoroterephthalonitrile) ([Alsbaiee et al., 2016](#_bookmark21)) and polymerised β-CD, epichlorohydrin and 2, 3-epoxypropyltrimethylammonium chlo-ride ([Hu et al., 2020](#_bookmark40)). In this paper, CD, chitosan, OH, aromatic units from perylene and ammonia cations are present, which provides a multifunctional character.

Based on results in [Table 4](#_bookmark13), the PSO model in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark12)B is the best fitting model due to an _R2_ value of 0.999. The PFO model in [Fig. 7](#_bookmark12)C does not provide good agreement with the _R2_ value of 0.906. Therefore, the description of kinetics for AO7 adsorption on the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite should be described with the PSO model.

- 1.  _Thermodynamic studies_

The thermodynamic parameters were determined through analysis of the adsorption process in the temperature range 20–60 ◦C. The pa-rameters were calculated from the relationship _lnKeq_ \= _f(1/T)_ ([Fig. 7](#_bookmark12)D), where _R2_ was 0.991, and indicates good agreement of data in [Table 5](#_bookmark14). At

every temperature, Δ_G0_ has a negative value (Δ_G0_ < 0), which refers to the spontaneous character of AO7 adsorption. Decreasing Δ_G0_ indicates

lower temperatures is thermodynamically preferred ([Crini, 2008](#_bookmark27); [Danesh et al., 2021](#_bookmark29); [Tu et al., 2020](#_bookmark70)). The strong negative value of _ΔH0_ supports the exothermic character of the process; thus, the temperature increase can induce a simultaneous desorption of AO7. In addition, the value below 40 kJ/mol indicates physical adsorption: hydrogen bonding, electrostatic forces (N+•••SO—), hydrophobic forces (CD-in-clusion complexation) ([Rizzi et al., 2021](#_bookmark62); [Yu et al., 2018](#_bookmark79)). The positive _ΔS0_ showed a random character at the solid-liquid interface between adsorbent and AO7; thus, the adsorbate molecules have freedom of motion towards the adsorption layer ([Danesh et al., 2021](#_bookmark29); [Konicki et al.,](#_bookmark49) [2013](#_bookmark49)).

[Fig. 8](#_bookmark15)A, the _A.E._ is maintained at a similar level of around 97–98 % for adsorption in a pH range of 6–9. The smaller decreases are observed for a pH range of 10–11 up to around 94 % of _A.E._, which can be connected to electrostatic repulsion between the hydroxyl anion and ammonia group of chitosan ([Rizzi et al., 2021](#_bookmark62)). The more acidic condition in a pH range of 3–5 results with greater decreases in values from 92.6 % to 79.9 % of

_A.E._ This situation can be caused by an interaction between H+ and

sulphonated groups of AO7 due to the formation of acidic intermediates that do not prefer electrostatic interactions in contrast to salt which forms. Thus, the pH does not strongly influence on AO7 adsorption in a pH range of 6–11 due to possible electrostatic interactions with AO7 anions and undisturbed hydrogen bonding.

The influence of the salt concentration was evaluated with the addition of NaCl as model salts in the concentration range of 0–0.5 M. The results in Fig. S8 shows a strong removal of AO7 even in highly salted solutions, up to 0.1 M with _A.E._ above 90 %. Only the 0.5 M concentration induce a decrease of up to 88.2 % of removal, which can be caused by the interaction of Cl— with the ammonia group of chitosan, and the cleavage of hydrogen bonding responsible for binding. This study indicates a possible lack of Na+ or Cl— ion adsorption, because lower concentrations would block and prevent adsorption of AO7 by the composite.

- 1.  _Selectivity assay_

Dye selectivity was performed on the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/ chitosan composite and pristine chitosan at a dye concentration of 100 mg/L in order to indicate the most favourable structure and compare behaviour between two adsorbents. The studied dyes were anionic dyes like AO7, MO and cationic dyes like MB or MG. The results presented in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark15)B indicates the highest removal for AO7 around 98.9 %. The removal of AO7 was 5 times greater than for chitosan. The MO was also efficiently removed at around 90 %, which is slightly lower than AO7 and 3.5 times greater than the chitosan. The removal of MB and MG were observed at around 10–13 %, indicating a strong preference of anionic dyes over cationic. On the other hand, the chitosan had a removal of 34–54 % for cationic dyes, which can be related to the structure of both materials and differences in interactions between adsorbent-adsorbate. In addition, the results for chitosan indicated the lower removal at around 17–26 % for anionic species.

The next studies focused on the evaluation of metal ions: Zn2+, Ni2+

and Cd2+, at a concentration of 10 mg/L ([Yaseen & Scholz, 2019](#_bookmark78)). As seen in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark15)B, the metal ions are barely removed with the composite, where _A.E._ resulted with 8.65 %, 10.8 % and 12 % for zinc, nickel and cadmium ions, respectively. It is much lower than dye removal like AO7 where 98.9 % of _A_._E_. was observed. This indicates the differentiation of adsorbent between anionic and cationic species of pollutants. On the other hand, native chitosan was able to remove 58.9 %, 47.7 % and 89.1

%. which is greater than the composite. Thus, the formed material has improved selective adsorption in comparison to native chitosan, pre-sumably due to the introduction of new binding sites and the reconfi-guration of the molecular structure with the CD polymer. This addition of CD induced the recognition of organic molecules over metal ions as well as the preference of anionic organic compounds over cationic.

Finally, studies for binary mixtures were carried out for AO7 and MB and the results are presented in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark15)C as the most efficiently removed anionic and cationic dyes, respectively. The novel adsorbent maintained a strong removal of AO7 with only a 3 % decrease in mixture, while for MB a weak removal with a 3 % decrease. The molecular recognition for AO7 was maintained even in binary mixtures, indicating the favouring of adsorbed dyes by their chemical character.

- 1.  _Reusability studies_

The initial experiments conducted to determine the most effective regeneration solution are illustrated in Fig. S9A. Mixtures of 0.01 M

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 8.** The effect of pH on adsorption efficiency (A). Selectivity assay for evaluation different pollutants in aqueous solutions - dyes concentration were 100 mg/L and metal ions concentration were 10 mg/L (B). Selectivity assay from one component solution and binary mixture (C). Reusability/recovery studies of the poly (β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite (D).

NaOH achieved a desorption rate of at least 66 %. In contrast, mixtures containing 0.01 M HCl exhibited a desorption rate of only 7–8 %, indicating a negative effect from HCl. This outcome suggests that NaOH effectively disrupted the electrostatic interactions between the cations in chitosan and the sulfonic group of AO7. Consequently, the dye was converted into its salt form; however, the presence of organic cosolvents helped to keep AO7 molecules in the regeneration mixture.

The highest desorption efficiency was observed with a methanol and

0.01 M NaOH mixture, which achieved around 85 % desorption. Ethanol and acetone resulted in 73 % and 66 % desorption efficiencies, respec-tively. Further studies aimed at optimizing the volume ratio between methanol and 0.01 M NaOH (see Fig. S9B) showed that the optimal ratio of 3:1 yielded the highest desorption at 85 %. Lower ratios (1:1 and 1:2) produced similar desorption efficiencies, likely due to insufficient organic solvent levels that could not prevent resorption onto the adsorbent. Conversely, the 4:1 ratio demonstrated a slight decrease in desorption, reaching around 72 %, presumably because the number of NaOH molecules was inadequate to interact effectively with the AO7 molecules on the adsorbent.

In order to determine the reusability and recovery abilities, adsorption-desorption cycles were evaluated 5 times. The most effective desorption mixture applied was the methanol/0.01 M NaOH in a volume

ratio 3:1. The methanol as part of the desorption mixture was considered due to the exothermic character (_ΔH0_ < 0) in aqueous solution.

The results in [Fig. 8](#_bookmark15)D show a very stable adsorption process through

3 cycles of around 98 % of _A.E._, while the 4th cycle decreased to 86.8 % and the 5th cycle to 80 %. The adsorbent seems to be capable of working

for many cycles and being reusable up to the efficient 5th cycle. On the other hand, the recovery efficiency slightly decreased after each step, presumably without fully eluted dyes. The desorption from the 1st cycles was 86.1 % and decreased to 68.9 % for the 5th cycle, could be con-nected to the interactions of unremoved dyes from previous cycles e.g. π-electrons, hydrogen bonding.

- 1.  _Adsorption-induced changes in pore structure_

The AO7 adsorption processes affected the pore structure in the poly (β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite. In the low-pressure nitro-gen adsorption studies (LPA), N2 adsorption isotherms (Fig. S10) were obtained, which had a similar shape in the composite both before and

after AO7 adsorption. According to IUPAC, they were classified as type II isotherms ([Lachowicz et al., 2023](#_bookmark50)). In the pressure range of 0 < p/p0 < 0.8, the free sorption sites were uniformly filled with adsorbate (N2), and above p/p0 = 0.8, the adsorption intensity increased. Such a shape of the isotherm proves that the largest pore volume in these materials is the

share of mesopores. The adsorption of AO7 did not change the nature of the composite pore space, however, the total N2 sorption capacity of the composite at standard temperature and pressure before sorption was about 4.3 cm3N2/g (Table S2), and after AO7 sorption it was 3.3 cm3N2/ g, respectively. The specific surface area according to Brunauer-Emmetta-Teller isotherm (SSABET) and Barrett-Joyner-Halend isotherm (SSABJH) values indicate that after AO7 adsorption, the available pore surface area was slightly reduced. Some of the previously free active sites were filled. The free pore volume was also reduced. It is worth

mentioning that this method characterises pores from the range of mi-cropores (0–2 nm) and the smallest mesopores (max. up to 50 nm), in which capillary condensation occurs. The small decrease in pore size is resultant in filling not only micropores but also mesopores. This pore size is average value from micro- and mesopores. Thus, the filling the micro- and mesopores by dye molecules results in small changes, some mesopores can become decreased to lowered pore sizes giving averaged pore size. In addition, adsorption of N2 depends more on physical adsorption, less likely as chemical which is favoured by this material. This experiments confirmed surface interactions between adsorbent-AO7, because there were changes in surface/pore structure during N2 adsorption.

- 1.  _Mechanism of adsorption_

The molecular mechanism of adsorption was studied with FT-IR spectroscopy for the composite before and after adsorption of AO7 ([Fig. 9](#_bookmark16)). The first significant change was observed at 3392 cm—1, after the adsorption band became less intensive and wider. This indicates the participation of O–H or N–H bonds in the adsorption process via hydrogen bonding of AO7 or even electrostatic interactions from NH+. The second change was observed for the band at 1562 cm—1 with a significant decrease of intensity corresponding to the NH+ bond from the

3

3

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

**Fig. 9.** Comparative analysis of FT-IR spectra for adsorption process of AO7 on the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite.

chitosan matrix. This suggests the electrostatic interactions of NH+ with the SO— group from AO7 ([Ostrowska-Czubenko & Gierszewska-Dru-z˙yn´ska, 2009](#_bookmark57)). The region 1158–1028 cm—1 is characterised with a less sharp shape and smaller intensities, thus the carbohydrate units are participating in the adsorption process, e.g. inclusion complexation in-side CD's cavity ([Qin et al., 2019](#_bookmark60)). Similar results can come from FT-IR spectra for biosorption of AO7 by canola waste, where hydrogen bonding and electrostatic were the main binding forces ([Balarak et al.,](#_bookmark23) [2020](#_bookmark23)). Another case was observed for hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions and π–π stacking between the MIL-101-SO3H@Graphene Oxide composite and azo dyes, especially AO7 ([Yang et al., 2024](#_bookmark77)) Similar composite based on polyvinyl alcohol and chitosan was also applied for removal AO7; the FT-IR spectroscopy showed hydrogen bonding as stabilizing force for composite as well as binding force be-tween composite and dye. In addition, the electrostatic interactions occurred during adsorption of dye ([Perez-Calderon et al., 2023](#_bookmark58)).

According to Table S1 and Fig. S11, the content of elements on the adsorbent surface is changing before and after adsorption. The content of all the elements is maintained on similar levels, but the Sulphur atoms appeared on the surface after adsorption. The content of Sulphur atoms is 0.8 % and comes from the AO7 possessing sulphonic group in its structure. It proves the adsorption mechanism of AO7 by the composite through surface interactions.

3

3

The differentiation of dyes by this composite can be induced by electrostatic interaction ([Jiang et al., 2019](#_bookmark45); [Lagiewka et al., 2023](#_bookmark51)), where a positively charged adsorbent strongly removes anionic dyes ([Li](#_bookmark52) [et al., 2018](#_bookmark52)). While the pristine chitosan does not possess charged groups and binds via hydrogen bonding with most types of pollutants. The presence of carboxylic from the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network did not have an effect on pollutant adsorption, but the addition allowed the formation of a new material with actively and selectively binding through charged amino groups contrary to the pristine chitosan.

Moreover, the calculated stoichiometry between CD cavities in the adsorbent and AO7 molecules is 1:16, which seems to avoid standard stoichiometry for native CD and guest molecules (1:1). However, the whole composite took part not only CD cavity forming bigger spaces for binding sorbate molecules. The CD cavities can serve more as building blocks, partially sharing guest molecules (especially branched, bulky like AO7), or forming supramolecular pores altogether (few CD cavities form supramolecular pores) ([Crini et al., 2022](#_bookmark28); [Lagiewka et al., 2023](#_bookmark51)). To sum up, the mechanism of AO7 removal by the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan composite is in [Fig. 10](#_bookmark17) and shows the complexity of the process. The binding of AO7 to the composite is based on adsorption, which characterises surface interactions for sorbent-

# Conclusions

In this study, the novel composite based on the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network and chitosan was obtained for the removal of anionic dyes. The composite contained novel the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network, which contained CD, perylene units and carboxylate groups. The formation of the composite was carried out via ionic crosslinking between the carboxylate group COO— and NH+ of polymers. The presented protocol indicated novel material preparation in two-steps without laborious conditions. The characterisation was performed with spectral, thermal, microscopic and X-ray methods. The aim of this study was achieved by the crosslinking of chitosan with the carboxylate polymer of CD. The most optimal composition of the composite was a mass ratio at 20 % of poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network and 80 % of chitosan matrix. The adsorp-tion capacity of AO7 was 384.61 mg/g according to Langmuir isotherm and the rapid removal resulted in 95.6 % after 1 min. The AO7 was the most removed anionic dyes, while the addition of the CD polymer induced the recognition of anionic over cationic dyes or metal ions. Additionally, the price of the adsorbent (1522 USD per kg) is compa-rable to native chitosan. Its five times higher adsorption effectiveness than native chitosan, along with rapid removal and selectivity, en-courages the preparation of this material for the removal of anionic dyes. The molecular mechanism of binding is based on surface interactions through electrostatic interaction, hydrogen bonding and inclusion complexation according to FT-IR analysis. The hypothesis was confirmed with following results: the addition of the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network to the chitosan matrix enhanced its removal efficiency by 5-times and its selectivity over other organic dyes or metal ions. To sum up, the poly(β-CD-PTCDA) network/chitosan is a promising adsorbent for efficient and rapid removal of anionic organic dyes from (waste) water.
